title: Foundation Models for Trading (Part III): Running a Generative AI Forecaster Inside MetaTrader 5
text:
Introduction
Across
Part 1
and
Part 2
, we built a complete native MQL5 port of Kronos and proved, stage by stage, that it reproduces the PyTorch model: exact encoder tokens, decoder and predictor logits within floating-point noise, and autoregressive generation verified through the context-sliding boundary. That answers only the easy question. Fidelity to PyTorch is not the same as forecasting skill. A faithful port of a model that cannot predict the market is still a model that cannot predict the market.
The distinction matters more than it might seem. Verification is a closed question with a right answer: either our matrices agree with the reference or they do not, and a tolerance of 1e-06 settles the argument. Forecasting skill is an open question with no reference to check against, only the market, which is happy to hand you a convincing-looking result that means nothing at all. The tools that settle the first question are useless for the second. The habits that made the port trustworthy, namely tight tolerances and exact comparisons, can also leave you overconfident when you switch to measuring value.
This part asks the hard question honestly. First, we put the model to work in the most satisfying way: an Expert Advisor that draws Kronos's forecast candles directly on the chart. This lets you watch it predict in real time. Then we stop admiring the picture and measure it. We dump forecasts across a stretch of history under strict look-ahead discipline, score them against a naive baseline, and run a deliberately simple strategy through the Strategy Tester. The result is a negative one, and reported plainly, because a negative result that is honestly arrived at is worth more than a positive one that is not.
The most useful thing the project produced is a lesson in reading a backtest. A simple rule on these forecasts ends in profit with a rising equity curve, and two plain checks, the spread of the trade results and a split of the trades by direction, show that the profit is the market's drift rather than anything the model knew.
We will cover:
Forecasting Live on the Chart
An Honest Evaluation and the Look-Ahead Problem
Forecast Skill Against a Random Walk
A Backtest That Profits Without an Edge
The Verdict, and Why
Conclusion
Forecasting Live on the Chart
The
KronosForecast
Expert Advisor attaches the model to a chart. On each new completed bar it gathers the last context window of candles, runs the full pipeline from Part 2, and paints the predicted bars to the right of the current price as forecast candles.
Inference is expensive: a full
Predict
at the real configuration takes seconds, which rules out running one per tick, so the Expert Advisor gates on the bar. SERIES_LASTBAR_DATE is the open time of the newest, still-forming bar, so it changes once per bar, at the moment a new bar opens and the previous one completes. The handler returns immediately while it matches the remembered value:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Tick handler: re-forecast only when a new bar has completed.     |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+

(t == g_last_bar)

// only on a new completed bar
g_last_bar = t;
   RunForecast();
  }
The work happens in
RunForecast
, which assembles the same raw window and time stamps the verification used and calls the single
Predict

The loop reads
rates[L]
down to
rates[1]
, never
rates[0]
, so the window holds
closed bars only
. The still-forming bar at index zero changes with every tick, and feeding it to the model would make the forecast depend on the moment you happened to look. The index reversal is deliberate too:
RunForecast
calls ArraySetAsSeries on
rates
before CopyRates fills it, so the array runs newest-first, and reading
rates[L - i]
puts the oldest bar in row zero, as the model expects.
The second point is volume. Two of Kronos's six features, volume and amount, do not exist in a retail FX feed, so we fill them from tick volume and a turnover of tick volume times the typical price. That turnover formula is the reference predictor's own fallback when it has volume but no amount. The problem is the volume itself: a tick count differs from exchange volume in scale and in distribution, and the per-window normalization removes only the scale. A third of the model's input therefore comes from a distribution it never saw in training, which will matter when we judge the forecast.
The stamp matrix hides a subtlety. Kronos conditions on time stamps as well as prices, and it wants one for every position, including the bars it is about to predict. Those bars have not happened, so their stamps are projected forward from the last known bar time:

Projecting

assumes a fixed grid of bars, which holds inside a session and fails across a weekend or holiday. A stamp that lands on a Saturday perturbs the temporal embedding for those positions, but it does not corrupt the price history, and it is not look-ahead: future time stamps are known in advance and say nothing about future prices. The effect can also be measured. In the evaluation below, 115 of the 947 forecasts cross a weekend, and the other 832, scored on their own, are still less accurate than the no-change baseline at every horizon. The projection does not decide the result.

Every object carries the
KronosFC_
prefix, which makes the routine's first line safe:
ObjectsDeleteAll
with that prefix clears the previous forecast without touching anything else on the chart, and
OnDeinit
clears it the same way. Setting
OBJPROP_RAY
to false keeps each trend line a finite segment rather than the default infinite ray.
Fig. 1. The KronosForecast Expert Advisor drawing the predicted candles to the right of the current price, refreshed on each new bar
It is a compelling picture, and that is precisely the danger. The forecast arrives as a clean, decisive sequence of candles with a shape and a direction, drawn in the same style as the real price beside it, and nothing in the rendering distinguishes a confident prediction from a coin flip. The model is equally happy to draw sixteen bars of nonsense. The rest of this part is about resisting that invitation and measuring whether the picture is worth anything.
An Honest Evaluation and the Look-Ahead Problem
Evaluating a forecasting model on market data is full of ways to fool yourself, and almost all of them reduce to one mistake: letting information from the future leak into a decision about the past. A backtest that peeks, even slightly, can turn a useless model into a brilliant one on paper. The leak is rarely deliberate. It arrives as an off-by-one in an array index, a bar that was not yet closed when it was read, or a series quietly recalculated over the full history before the walk begins. So the evaluation is built around a strict separation, and the architecture is chosen to make leakage structurally hard rather than merely promised.
The design has three pieces, run in order: a script that walks history once and dumps forecasts to a file, a script that reads the file and reports forecast quality with no trading, and an Expert Advisor that reads the same file and runs a strategy in the Strategy Tester.
Splitting it this way is partly a matter of cost, though less than you might expect. Part 2's headline figure was a full
Predict
in about sixteen seconds, measured with five sampled paths. The dump runs a single greedy path instead. At the same 256-bar context, one autoregressive step costs about 200 milliseconds, and a sixteen-bar forecast takes sixteen of them plus the encoding and decoding around them. Measured across the full run, a forecast came to just under five seconds, so 947 evaluation bars took about an hour and a quarter of uninterrupted computation. That is enough to rule out running inference inside the Strategy Tester, where every threshold change would pay the whole bill again. But the more important reason is discipline. Because the model runs once and writes its output to a file, everything downstream reads the same fixed numbers, and no analysis can accidentally change what the model predicted. Running the dump with greedy decoding rather than sampling completes the picture: the forecasts become deterministic, so the entire study reproduces exactly rather than approximately.
That choice deserves one caveat stated up front rather than buried. Greedy decoding is not the mode the chart Expert Advisor runs in, and it is not the mode the reference implementation uses either: both draw sampled paths and average them, five of them in the figure above. Greedy takes the highest-probability token at every step, so it traces the single most likely trajectory instead of the center of the distribution. Averaging many sampled paths approximates that same center, which is why we do not expect the verdict to move, but we did not separately verify it, and we would rather say so than let the reader assume the two were tested. What follows is a statement about greedy Kronos on this data.

Two months of EURUSD H1, every bar, with a 256-bar context and a 16-bar horizon. The window is modest because forecasting is the expensive step, and it is trivial to extend. It yields 947 forecasts, just over fifteen thousand individual predictions to score, though, as we will see, far fewer independent ones.
Look-ahead prevention starts with how much history the script requests. Each evaluation bar needs a full context
behind
it and the realized bars
ahead
of it, so the copy range is padded on both sides:
//--- Pull enough history: L bars before the start, P bars after the end, so
//--- every eval bar has a full context AND P realized bars. Oldest-first.
datetime
from = InpStartDate - (
datetime
)((L +
2
) * secs);
datetime
to   = InpEndDate   + (
datetime
)((P +
2
) * secs);
   MqlRates rates[];
int
got =
CopyRates
(
_Symbol
,
_Period
, from, to, rates);
The array stays oldest-first, with no series flag, which is the orientation the model expects and removes a whole class of index-reversal bugs. The padding lets the walk treat every bar identically, with no special cases at the edges, which is exactly where leaks hide.
The padding is measured in calendar seconds while the loop counts bars. Stepping back 258 hours from the first of April reaches the twenty-first of March, but weekends remove about a third of those hours from an H1 series, so the 256th bar of the fetched array lands several days into the requested window. The first forecast is therefore keyed at 2025.04.04 rather than 2025.04.01, which costs a few evaluation bars and nothing else. Too little history is the safe direction to err in: a bar without a full context is skipped, never forecast from a short one.
The walk itself then reduces to a single indexed loop, and the comment above it states the whole look-ahead argument in two lines:
//--- Eval bar t: context is rates[t-L+1 .. t], ending at t's close (the anchor),
//--- and forecasts cover t+1..t+P. Nothing at or after t+1 feeds the forecast.
int

0

t0 =

();

(
int

1
; t + P < got; t++)

(rates[t].time < InpStartDate || rates[t].time > InpEndDate)

;

(((t - L +
1
) % InpStep) !=
0

datetime
ctx_time[];
      BuildWindow(rates, t - L +
1
, L, raw, ctx_time);
// closed bars t-L+1..t
The bound
t + P < got
means a bar is evaluated only if all P of its future bars exist, so no forecast is scored against missing bars. The context passed to
BuildWindow
is
rates[t-L+1 .. t]
, the L closed bars ending at the evaluation bar itself, so the last candle the model sees is the one whose close is the anchor. Nothing at or after
t+1
touches the forecast.
The window has to end exactly there, and the opposite error is harder to notice. End it one bar early, at
t-1
, and the model's first forecast is of bar
t
, yet it is scored against bar
t+1
from a close the model never saw. Nothing leaks, so no look-ahead check flags it, but every horizon is scored one bar out of step and the model is penalized for information it was never given. The forecasts are identical either way, only keyed one bar apart, so only the indices give it away.
The realized future closes go into the same row, purely so the quality script can score against them. The writing routine states that contract in the file itself:

//| One row: eval-bar time, its close, forecast closes 1..P, then the|
//| REALIZED future closes 1..P (rates[t+1..t+P]). Stored for scoring|
//| only, never an input to any forecast/trade decision.             |

int
fh,
const
MqlRates &rates[],

matrix &forecast)

, forecast[h][
3

// col 3 = close

int

1

StringFormat
(
",%.6f"
, rates[t + h].close);
FileWrite
(fh, row);
  }
Storing the answer next to the prediction feels wrong at first glance, and it is worth being clear about why it is safe. The realized closes occupy their own columns, written after the forecast was already computed, and the two consumers treat them very differently. The quality script reads them because scoring is exactly the act of comparing a prediction to what happened. The signal Expert Advisor, as we will see, reads the forecast columns and explicitly discards the realized ones. The separation is enforced by which columns each program keeps. That is a structural guarantee, not a promise.
Fig. 2. One evaluation bar. The context is the L closed bars ending at it, its close is the anchor, the forecast covers the P bars after it, and the realized bars are read only when scoring, never when forecasting or trading
The look-ahead guard, stated plainly:
context uses only bars at or before the evaluation bar; forecasts cover the bars after it; realized future closes are stored only to score against, never fed into a decision; and the strategy, when it runs, enters at the next bar's open, not on the bar it reads. Information only ever flows forward.
Forecast Skill Against a Random Walk
The cleanest measure of a forecast involves no strategy at all: no threshold, no sizing, no stop loss, and so no parameter combination to stumble on. The
KronosEvalQuality
script reads the dump and asks two questions for each horizon from 1 to 16 bars. Does the predicted direction match the realized one more often than a rule that ignores the model? And is the predicted return closer to the truth than a random walk, the naive prediction that the price will not move?
That baseline is the crux of the whole evaluation. On liquid intraday FX, "no change" is a famously hard prediction to beat, because the next move really is close to unpredictable and the current price is already the market's best estimate of the next one. A forecasting model does not earn its keep by being roughly right about the level, which the previous close achieves for free. It earns its keep by beating that baseline, and any model that cannot is worse than doing nothing.
The accumulators keep both errors side by side, per horizon, so the comparison is always made on identical samples:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Per-horizon running accumulators.                                |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
struct
HorizonStat
  {
int
n;
// directional samples (actual and forecast both non-flat)
int
dir_hit;
// Kronos directional hits
int
up;
// realized up-moves among those samples
double
k_abs;
// sum |kronos_ret - actual_ret|
double
k_sq;
// sum (kronos_ret - actual_ret)^2
double
rw_abs;
// sum |0 - actual_ret| == sum |actual_ret|
double
rw_sq;
// sum actual_ret^2
};
Working in returns rather than prices keeps the numbers comparable while the level drifts. As the dump is loaded, every forecast and realized close becomes a cumulative return from the anchor close:
for
(
int
h =
0
; h < P; h++)
        {
         g_k[g_rows * P + h] = (fc[h] - last_close) / last_close;
// predicted cumulative return to h
g_a[g_rows * P + h] = (ac[h] - last_close) / last_close;
// realized   cumulative return to h
}
The scoring routine walks those returns and accumulates the two error series. It takes a list of row indices rather than reading the rows in order, for a reason that becomes clear when we measure the uncertainty:
double
k_ret = g_k[base + h];
double
a_ret = g_a[base + h];
//--- directional accuracy: skip flat actuals (no direction to call)
//--- and flat forecasts (no call made)
if
(a_ret !=
0.0
&& k_ret !=
0.0
)
           {
if
((k_ret >
0.0
) == (a_ret >
0.0
)) st[h].dir_hit++;
if
(a_ret >
0.0
) st[h].up++;
            st[h].n++;

double
k_err = k_ret - a_ret;
         st[h].k_abs +=
MathAbs
(k_err);
         st[h].k_sq  += k_err * k_err;
         st[h].rw_abs +=
MathAbs
(a_ret);
// baseline error == |actual return|
st[h].rw_sq  += a_ret * a_ret;
Predicting "no change" means predicting a zero return, so the baseline's error
is
whatever the price did, and
rw_abs
simply accumulates the absolute realized return. The directional count skips flat realized closes, which have no direction to call, and flat forecasts, which make no call. That is why it comes to 15,121 rather than the 15,152 that 947 forecasts at sixteen horizons would give: twenty-three realized closes landed exactly on the anchor, and eight forecasts did. The error sums run over every forecast and are divided by the forecast count, not the directional count.
The
up
field supplies a second directional baseline. A coin flip scores 50%, but in a window where the price mostly rose, a rule that always calls "up" scores more without any model. The share of realized up-moves per horizon is that rule's score, and a forecaster has to beat it, not just the coin.
The report then turns the two error sums into one ratio per horizon, the number that settles the question:

0.0

0

0.0

PrintFormat
(
"%2d| %6.2f%%  %5.1f%% | %.6f %.6f %5.3f | %.6f %.6f %5.3f"
,
                  h +
1
, diracc *
100.0
, upshr *
100.0
, k_rmse, rw_rmse, rmse_skill,
                  k_mae, rw_mae, mae_skill);

Both skill ratios exceed 1.0 at every horizon, so the point forecasts are less accurate than assuming the price will not move, and the two error measures agree everywhere, so the result is not an artifact of squaring the errors. Directional accuracy is 51.83% overall across 15,121 scored predictions, which looks like a sliver of skill until it is set beside the up-move column. For the first nine horizons the price rose 53% to 54% of the time, so always predicting "up" would have beaten Kronos at every one of them. Only from eleven bars out, where the up share falls to around 50%, does the model edge ahead of the majority call, by 1.5 to 3.3 points.
The skill column stays in a narrow band between 1.07 and 1.13 from one bar to ten, least bad at 1.071 at seven bars, then climbs to 1.403 at sixteen. Near the anchor the model adds a steady amount of error to a baseline that is already as good as it gets on near-random hourly moves; further out, sixteen bars of accumulated autoregressive drift carry the forecast away from the price.
How Much Evidence the Sample Holds
The rise in directional accuracy at the longest horizons is tempting, but the samples overlap heavily. Stepping one bar at a time, each 16-bar forecast shares fifteen of its bars with its neighbour, so consecutive rows nearly repeat the same measurement, and treating them as independent would overstate the confidence of every number in the table.
The script measures this with a
moving-block bootstrap

A skeptic might still ask whether a simple trading rule could extract something the error metrics miss. It is not an unreasonable question. A model can be poorly calibrated on average and still be informative when it speaks loudly, and directional accuracy weights every prediction equally when a trader would not. So we built a rule, deliberately trivial, so that any result reflects the model and not clever strategy engineering.

InpThreshold

The two thresholds are placed by the model's own output. At sixteen bars, 69.6% of forecasts predict a move above 0.1%, so that threshold trades on most bars. Only 5.2% predict a move above 0.6%, so that threshold keeps only the loudest calls, where a model poorly calibrated on average might still be informative. They represent those two regimes, and we report both rather than the better one.
Both runs cover a tester range spanning the dump's window on EURUSD H1, and the tradeable span inside it shows the look-ahead rules at work. The first forecast is keyed at 2025.04.04 21:00, for the calendar-versus-bars reason above. The last is keyed at 2025.05.30 07:00, a Friday, because no later bar could have sixteen realized bars ahead of it before the weekend. Outside that span the row lookup finds nothing and the Expert Advisor stands aside, so the dump alone defines the experiment.
The runs use the "Open prices only" model, sufficient because the Expert Advisor acts only as a bar opens, with a $10,000 deposit, 1:500 leverage and a fixed 0.1 lot, so a dollar of profit is a pip of EURUSD movement. The tester charges this account's real costs: the spread recorded in the price history, about two points as measured from the fills, a commission of $0.70 per round turn, and overnight swap. One detail links back to the shadow flag. In this mode the tick that opens a 00:00 bar can precede the trading session, and an order sent on it is rejected with [Market closed]. That happened eleven times in the fair run, and because the Expert Advisor reads its position from the terminal, each rejection simply left it where it was.
With the high threshold of 0.6%, the strategy acts only eight times in two months. Four trades win, the Profit Factor is 0.66, and the run ends $73.60 down before costs. Eight trades cannot support a conclusion either way. That is the tester's first lesson, and it cuts both ways: on a different two months the same handful of trades could as easily have drawn a smooth rising curve.

The rows from the Profit Factor down are the tester's own figures, after costs. At face value the fair run is a modest success: a Profit Factor of 1.05, a Sharpe ratio of 0.34, and an equity curve that ends higher than it started.
Fig. 4. The fair-threshold backtest: 133 trades and a small profit after costs, which the checks below trace to the market's drift
Two checks take that success apart. The first is the spread of the results. Before costs the strategy made $220.20 over 133 trades, $1.66 per trade, against a per-trade standard deviation of $40.29: a t-statistic of 0.47, far below any conventional threshold. Resampling the trades with replacement gives a result of zero or worse in about 31% of resamples, and the Z-Score of -0.80 says the order of wins and losses is indistinguishable from chance.
The second check asks where the profit came from. The 68 long trades made $328.70; the 65 short trades lost $108.50. EURUSD rose from about 1.094 to 1.135 over the window, roughly 3.7%, so a rule that takes about half its trades long collects part of that rise whatever its signal says. It is the same drift that let the always-up rule beat the model in the quality study, now showing up as money.
Costs take most of what is left. Commission and swap come to $130.61, about 59% of the profit before costs, the commission a fixed $0.70 per round turn regardless of the signal, and a wider live spread would cost more again. With $1.66 per trade there is little room for any of it. The extremes agree: the largest loss, $272.89, is over two and a half times the largest win of $105.75, because with no stops a directionless signal leaves large adverse moves unprotected.
Before believing a profitable backtest, ask what it would have made without the model.
Count the trades, compare the average result with the spread of results, and split the trades by direction. A small profit that lives on the long side of a rising market is the market's drift, whatever the headline metrics say.
The Verdict, and Why
Three views of the same 947 forecasts agree. The point forecasts are less accurate than no change at every horizon, with intervals above the baseline. The directional calls are indistinguishable from 50% and, at short horizons, lose to always calling "up". The backtest's profit is indistinguishable from zero and comes from the long side of a rising market. The views are not independent, since all three read the same forecasts over the same two months, but they ask different questions.
Two separate claims follow. Over this window of EURUSD H1, greedy Kronos shows no forecasting skill over the no-change baseline, and the simple rule built on its forecasts shows no trading edge. The reasons are specific and instructive rather than a failure of the port:
Domain mismatch.
Kronos was trained on equities and crypto, largely on daily and longer bars. We fed it hourly foreign-exchange data, a different instrument class on a different time scale from the one it learned. Foundation models generalize within their domain far better than across it, and hourly FX is a long way from daily equities in both statistical character and market structure.
Synthetic volume.
FX feeds carry no real exchange volume, so we manufactured the volume and amount features from tick volume and a derived turnover. The model has never seen those proxies; two of its six input features are, to it, out of distribution, and it has no way to signal that it is less certain because of it.
A brutal baseline.
EURUSD intraday is close to a martingale, where the next move is nearly unpredictable and "no change" is an extremely strong baseline. Beating it on this instrument at this scale is hard for any forecaster, and a skill ratio of 1.07 even at the model's best horizon is the price of insisting on a direction where none is reliably available.
We deliberately did not go looking for a kinder setup to produce a greener number. A retest on daily bars with real exchange volume, closer to where Kronos was actually trained, is the obvious follow-up and might well tell a different story. But running it only after a disappointing result and reporting only the better of the two is the exact dishonesty this evaluation was built to avoid. The verdict stands as the worst-case-but-fair one, and the retest, if anyone runs it, belongs alongside this result rather than instead of it.

The teaching point:
verification proved the port is faithful to PyTorch and said nothing about market edge. Trading-model write-ups most often mislead by presenting the first as the second, and a backtest that turns the market's drift into a rising equity curve is that trap in its most ordinary form.
Conclusion
This series set out to run a real foundation model natively inside MetaTrader 5 and to find out honestly whether it was any good. The port is faithful, proven against PyTorch at every stage. The forecasts, greedy-decoded on two months of EURUSD H1 with synthesized volume, carry no usable edge, and three views of them, each asking a different question, agree.
The forecast is verifiable and useless here, at once.
Faithful to the reference, and without market edge on this instrument. Holding both facts honestly is the point, and neither one weakens the other.
A profit is not an edge.
The fair backtest ends in profit, and the profit is noise plus the market's drift: indistinguishable from zero, and earned on the long side of a rising market. Counting the trades, comparing the average result with the spread, and splitting by direction is what tells the two apart.
Alignment is part of honesty.
Look-ahead is the famous error, but a context window that stops one bar short leaks nothing and still scores every forecast at the wrong horizon. Only the indices reveal it.
Architecture can enforce honesty.
Dumping forecasts offline, scoring them in a separate script, and having the Expert Advisor discard the realized columns as it parses makes look-ahead structurally difficult rather than a matter of good intentions. Reading position state from the terminal instead of a shadow flag is the same instinct applied to a smaller problem.
Honest negatives compound into trust.
The reasons the model fails here, domain and time-scale mismatch and synthetic volume, are concrete, and they point at exactly the retest that would be fair to try next.
That closes the series. Running a foundation model in MQL5 turned out to be the tractable part: three articles in, the engine works, it is verified, and it is fast enough to use. Knowing whether to trust what it says is the whole game, and the discipline that answered it, verify fidelity and market value separately, refuse to let the future leak into the past, and ask what a backtest would have made without the model before believing it, is the part worth carrying to the next model. The engine outlives this particular negative result, and so does the method for judging the next one.
The programs presented in this article are intended for educational purposes only. The evaluation reported here is a specific, honest negative result for greedy decoding on one instrument, one time frame and one two-month window, with synthesized volume; it is not investment advice and does not imply the model would behave the same way in other settings. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

against: The model uses synthetic volume and amount features derived from tick volume, which do not exist in retail spot FX data (no real exchange volume, no turnover); this violates condition (3): 'need data which is not available in spot forex'. The article explicitly states: 'Two of Kronos's six features, volume and amount, do not exist in a retail FX feed, so we fill them from tick volume and a turnover of tick volume times the typical price' and 'a third of the model's input therefore comes from a distribution it never saw in training'.

The forecasting model is trained on equities and crypto (daily+ bars), but applied to hourly EURUSD — a domain and time-scale mismatch that fundamentally breaks input distribution assumptions; however, this is *not* a fatal port flaw per the defined criteria (it’s a data/assumption mismatch, not an unimplementable rule or look-ahead). So it belongs in non_fatal.

The trading signal uses a threshold on predicted return at a fixed horizon (e.g., 'if pred_ret > InpThreshold go long'), but the article does *not specify any concrete, self-contained formula for entry/exit logic beyond this generic threshold rule* — crucially, it gives *no objective, deterministic condition for when to exit*, only 'hold for the horizon or until the signal flips', and 'signal flip' depends on future forecasts not yet computed at entry time. However, the EA *does* implement a concrete rule: it acts on forecast keyed at previous bar, holds for InpHorizon bars, and exits/reverses only when new forecast contradicts current position. That *is* objectively implementable. So no fatal (2) violation.

No use of martingale, grid, or averaging losses — explicitly avoided: 'no stops, targets or filters', 'no stops' mentioned, and trades are flat-or-one-position, closed before reversing. So (4) does not apply.

This *is* a trading rule article (not infrastructure/graphic/optimizer/example): it presents a full signal generation pipeline (forecast → threshold → entry/exit logic), backtest, and evaluation. So (5) does not apply.

No look-ahead in signal: article explicitly enforces 'context uses only bars at or before the evaluation bar', 'forecast keyed at the PREVIOUS bar', 'decision never uses information from the bar it trades on', and 'realized closes [...] discarded'. So (1) does not apply.
non_fatal: Domain mismatch: model trained on equities/crypto (daily+), applied to hourly FX — affects generalization but not implementability.

Synthetic volume/amount: as above — critical data fidelity issue, but not 'data unavailable in spot forex' *in the strict sense*? Wait: article says 'volume and amount do not exist in a retail FX feed', and tick volume ≠ exchange volume — so this *is* (3). Already listed in 'against'.
No stop-loss or take-profit logic — but the criteria do *not* require them; absence is non-fatal.
No out-of-sample test reported by author — but per instructions, 'absence of test outside sample [...] NOT considered fatal'.
No accounting for spread/commission in core forecast evaluation — explicitly excluded from fatal flaws per instructions.
Use of greedy decoding instead of sampling (which chart EA uses) — acknowledged caveat, but not a fatal flaw: still a well-defined, deterministic rule.

Evaluation window crosses weekends/holidays with naive time projection — but article states 'it does not corrupt the price history, and it is not look-ahead', and tests show result unchanged — so non-fatal.

Условие входа формально описано как 'если прогнозируемый возврат превышает порог — вход в лонг, если ниже отрицательного порога — вход в шорт', однако: (1) порог InpThreshold не задан фиксированным значением в статье — он указан как параметр, выбираемый автором (0.1% или 0.6%), но не обоснован как часть правила; (2) ключевой параметр InpHorizon = 16 — это горизонт прогноза, а не длительность удержания позиции в барах: в коде указано 'hold for the horizon or until the signal flips', но 'signal flip' определяется новым прогнозом на следующем баре, который зависит от будущих данных и не может быть вычислен заранее при входе — это делает выход недетерминированным и неформализуемым как правило на закрытом баре; (3) модель использует два признака (объём и объём*цена), которые прямо заявлены как 'не существующие в ритейл-спот-Форексе' и заменены синтетическими аналогами (tick volume + typical price), что нарушает условие применимости: данные, необходимые для расчёта сигнала, недоступны в стандартных спот-форекс-источниках без модификации/подмены. Это фатальный порок по критерию 'неприменимые данные'.

judge.summary: Статья представляет инфраструктурную реализацию генеративной ИИ-модели Kronos в MetaTrader 5 и её применение для прогнозирования EURUSD H1, но не предлагает самостоятельное, полностью детерминированное торговое правило. Автор честно демонстрирует отсутствие прогнозной силы модели на этом инструменте и временном масштабе, объясняя провал доменным несоответствием и использованием синтетических признаков.
